series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/4] block: do not issue background swap bios as root
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series proposes a change to the block layer, specifically to the bio_issue_as_root_blkg() function. The goal is to prevent background swap bios from being issued as root, which bypasses cgroup IO controllers and can lead to memory deadlocks. This is done by introducing a new condition that checks for REQ_BACKGROUND in addition to REQ_SWAP.

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Identified potential issue with using REQ_BACKGROUND to mark swap bios as non-urgent, suggesting that this could lead to throttling and foreground paging. The author agreed that zswap writebacks are best effort and can tolerate failure.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 10:18:36AM +0200, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> bio_issue_as_root_blkg() issues every REQ_SWAP bio as root, bypassing
> the cgroup IO controllers, because reclaim cannot stall indefinitely on
> swap writes. Some swap writes are not urgent though: zswap writeback is
> best effort.
> 
> Such a bio cannot simply drop REQ_SWAP: dm-crypt and dm-thin rely on it
> for limit_swap_bios, which caps in-flight swap bios to avoid a memory
> deadlock, see commit a666e5c05e7c ("dm: fix deadlock when swapping to
> encrypted device").

Is that true?  REQ_BACKGROUND very much implies the I/O can the throttled
and thus better not be foreground paging, and thus the caller should be
able to tolerate a failure.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/4] mm/zswap: turn shrink_memcg_cb()'s argument into a flags word
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `shrink_memcg_cb()` function in the zswap module to accept a flags word instead of a boolean pointer as an argument. The flags word allows callers to pass additional information, specifically whether the walk stopped at an entry already in the swap cache. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather provides a more flexible way for callers to interact with the function. The patch defines a new flag `ZSWAP_SHRINK_SWAPCACHE` and updates the function's logic accordingly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/4] mm/zswap: allow writeback to be throttled by the cgroup IO controllers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the cgroup IO controllers to throttle zswap writeback operations by introducing a new 'throttled' flag in the swap_io_ctx structure. When this flag is set, the write operation is issued as background I/O instead of being exempt from cgroup throttling, which avoids priority inversion and ensures that memory reclaim is not stalled for other workloads.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] mm/zswap: move reclaim-driven writeback to a kworker
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the reclaim-driven writeback of zswap to a kworker, which writes back data in chunks of SWAP_CLUSTER_MAX entries at a time while holding a reference on the memcg. This change is made to prevent stalls caused by uninterruptible sleeps when the owning cgroup's IO budget is exceeded. The shrinker now reports nothing freed until the worker has run and completed the writeback.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the deferred writeback workers hold a reference on the memcg and requested that queued ones be stopped before calling zswap_memcg_offline_cleanup() to prevent potential issues.

Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that the patch introduces a single work item per lruvec on shrink_wq, which may not scale with multiple tasks entering direct reclaim due to idempotent writeback submission, and questioned whether proactive reclaimer and kswapd also need deferred writeback submission.

The reviewer noted that the deferred writeback mechanism will affect the shrinker control loop, causing the accumulation of writebacks to grow over time due to the changed behavior in shrinker_count() and shrinker_scan(), and requested a check be made in do_shrink_slab() in mm/shrinker.c.

Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that the patch changes a single-threaded workqueue to a multi-threaded one and suggested adding a mention of this change to the changelog.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 9:23 AM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:

I understand the problem this patch is trying to solve, but this
solution seems more involved than the changelog suggests :)

---

Ahhh, so it's one work-item (added to the shared shrink_wq)
per-lruvec, not one kworker or thread per-lruvec.

Hmm, supposed multiple tasks in a cgroup enter direct reclaim. In the
past, the amount of writeback submission will scale with the number of
tasks entering reclaim. But now, it's just a single work item
per-lruvec - IIUC, the submission of his work item is idempotent, so
it wouldn't scale like that anymore, right? I haven't wrapped quite
wrapped my head around this, but this sounds like a non-trivial
effect...

Also, do we need to defer writeback submission for proactive
reclaimer? Or kswapd? Only direct reclaimers have concerns with the
latency blowup from the throttling right?

There are a couple more behavioural changes, without proper
justifcation or mentioning in the changelog. More details inlined
below:

---

This will have effect on the shrinker control loop too, right?
Shrinker API accumulates the number of writebacks overtime based on
shrinker_count()'s output, and we serve that number of writebacks
throgh shrinker_scan(). With this basically that accumulation just
grows over time, correct? Check do_shrink_slab() in mm/shrinker.c...

Feels like this completely breaks that control loop.

---

This turns a single-threaded workqueue into multi-threaded workqueue, IIUC.

Worth at least an callout in the changelog?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the performance of zswap shrinker on systems running iocost by addressing two issues: (1) zswap writeback is issued as root and charged to the cgroup afterwards, causing stalls in application allocations; and (2) throttled writes sleep in their submitter, often an application thread. The patches modify zswap to mark writebacks as REQ_BACKGROUND instead of REQ_SWAP, allowing them to be throttled by iocost controllers. Additionally, patch 4 moves reclaim-driven writeback to a per-lruvec kworker, reducing the impact on application threads. The series includes benchmarks showing significant performance improvements for various workloads.

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Christoph Hellwig questioned whether REQ_BACKGROUND truly allows for throttling of I/O operations, suggesting that it implies the operation can be throttled and thus the caller should not expect foreground paging.
sentiment_signals: requested clarification on I/O throttling implications
review_comments.raw_body:
Is that true?  REQ_BACKGROUND very much implies the I/O can the throttled
and thus better not be foreground paging, and thus the caller should be
able to tolerate a failure.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the shrinker writeback should be done in a way that allows for proper accounting of IO costs, and suggested using iocost's throttling mechanism to control the rate at which writebacks occur.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti questioned the necessity of marking zswap writebacks as REQ_BACKGROUND, citing that they are already best effort and failure does not impact the compressed entry's presence.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Christoph,

On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 11:44 AM Christoph Hellwig <hch@infradead.org> wrote:

---

Yes, I agree, zswap writebacks are only best effort and in case of
failure, the compressed entry still lives. I don't see how
REQ_BACKGROUND could be an issue there?

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern about the scalability of adding multiple kworker threads for zswap writeback, suggesting alternatives such as per-cpu or global threading and inquiring about work accounting from a cgroup perspective.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yeah that tracks with an older experiment of mine, where I add some
manual throttling to zswap shrinker to reduce latency :) So I think
this problem is real - thanks for root-causing this, Alex!

I'm a bit nervous about adding multiple kworker threads though, hmmm.
Per-lruvec sounds like a lot of threads... Do we have to scale this by
lruvec? Why not per-cpu, or just a global thread? Is there any data to
support this autoscaling?

And do we have any concerns with work (CPU) accounting, from a cgroup
perspective...?

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 6/6] btrfs: find_free_extent checks size class unlocked

version_history.subject: [PATCH 6/6] btrfs: find_free_extent checks size class unlocked

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the find_free_extent function in Btrfs to skip block groups that have an incorrect size class without acquiring a lock on them. This change is intended to improve performance by reducing the number of locks taken, especially when dealing with large file systems containing thousands of block groups. The patch also includes benchmark results showing improved performance after applying this modification.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 5/6] btrfs: find_free_extent checks full block groups unlocked

version_history.subject: [PATCH 5/6] btrfs: find_free_extent checks full block groups unlocked

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the find_free_extent function in Btrfs by skipping block groups that are full and cannot satisfy an allocation request without taking a lock. This is done because checking if a block group can satisfy an allocation does not guarantee that it will be able to do so when locked, and racing with a free operation would result in the same outcome. The patch improves performance on large filesystems with many full block groups by reducing the number of unnecessary checks. Performance measurements show significant improvements in sequential 1G fallocates and sync operations after creating new files.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 4/6] btrfs: factor the find_free_extent() block group skip into a helper

version_history.subject: [PATCH 4/6] btrfs: factor the find_free_extent() block group skip into a helper

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors a complex block of code in the btrfs find_free_extent() function into a separate helper function called find_free_extent_skip_block_group(). This helper function checks if a block group can be skipped during the search for free extents, and returns true if it should be skipped. The original code has been simplified by removing duplicated logic and making it easier to understand.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 3/6] btrfs: remove redundant checks in find_free_extent() hint path

version_history.subject: [PATCH 3/6] btrfs: remove redundant checks in find_free_extent() hint path

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch removes redundant checks in the find_free_extent() function's hint path, making it more efficient by only checking for the unique condition that applies to hints. The hint is a long-lasting reference to a block group and must be checked if it's still attached to the list of block groups. Other checks are not specific to hints and can be shared with normally reached block groups. This change improves performance without compromising data integrity.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 2/6] btrfs: don't take block group references in find_free_extent()

version_history.subject: [PATCH 2/6] btrfs: don't take block group references in find_free_extent()

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the find_free_extent() function in Btrfs by removing unnecessary get/put pairs on block group references. The loop in this function is already protected by a semaphore, making it impossible for the reference count to be the last one. This change saves time on filesystems with many full block groups and reduces the overhead of refcounting.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 1/6] btrfs: skip unhelpful size class relaxing allocation loops

version_history.subject: [PATCH 1/6] btrfs: skip unhelpful size class relaxing allocation loops

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the Btrfs allocation loop by skipping unnecessary iterations when size class relaxation is not beneficial. It achieves this by tracking whether a block group was skipped due to its size class and only running loops that are relevant. This change aims to improve performance by reducing the number of unnecessary allocations. The approach taken involves modifying the `find_free_extent_update_loop` function to check for the `size_class_skipped` flag before running certain loops, and updating the `find_free_extent` function to set this flag when a block group is skipped due to its size class.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/6] btrfs: allocator perf improvements
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves the performance of the Btrfs allocator by reducing unnecessary operations on large file systems. Specifically, it optimizes the allocation process to skip unhelpful size class relaxing loops and redundant checks in the find_free_extent function. This results in significant speedup for certain workloads, such as running 20k fallocates in a loop on a sparse file system, from ~40s to ~7s.

review_comments.author: Sun YangKai
review_comments.summary: reviewer suggested using a more efficient method, such as sorting block groups by free space, to improve the lookup process in allocation
sentiment_signals: wondered if current approach is worthy
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Boris,

Glad to see this patchset resolves the long existing blockgroup 
allocator performance issue and I'm really impressed by the numbers of 
performance improvement.

IMO we currently go along the list to look for a proper bg that have 
enough free space, which means we may have to go through thousands of 
bgs during the allocation, I wonder if it is worthy to use a more 
efficient method like something sorted by bg's free space to improve the 
lookup process?

Please correct me if I got anything wrong.

And thanks for bringing these great patches.

Sun Yangkai

review_comments.author: Boris Burkov (author)
review_comments.summary: Author Boris Burkov addressed a concern about implementing gap size indexing at the block group level, explaining that it would introduce contention due to a write lock on the global ordering of block groups. He suggested alternative solutions such as batching or queuing work to update the ordering, and expressed interest in considering Martin's patch for scalability improvements.
sentiment_signals: considered this while working on size class stuff some years ago
I think that at least rules out naive solutions
review_comments.raw_body:
I considered this while working on the size class stuff some years ago.
If you look into the free space cache inside each block group, it does
in fact index by gap size as well as gap offset.

However if you do that at the block group level, then each allocation
requires a write to the global ordering of block groups so that means
having many parallel allocating threads now requires them to fight over
a write lock on that ordered structure. I think that at least rules out
naive solutions.

You could probably resolve it with some more clever scheme like batching
or queuing the work to update the ordering, or maybe some duplicated
view with atomic cut overs.

If you are interested in allocator performance, another thing we should
consider is resurrecting more of
https://lore.kernel.org/linux-btrfs/0102019bb2ff5805-8aa151b8-1fe7-4087-9610-4c3314b3b144-000000@eu-west-1.amazonses.com/

I actually didn't realize that Martin had hit a few of the same things
in that series so now I feel a bit bad about not working harder to
incorporate his work earlier.

If this series of mine goes in, we are ok on the put/get part since I
just got rid of it, and I was planning to get rid of data_rwsem after
https://lore.kernel.org/linux-btrfs/20260916-btrfs-remove-v1-space-cache-v3-0-10ebde03b96f@columbia.edu/
goes in. But I have not tried to tackle the scalability of groups_sem
yet, and would probably start by seriously evaluating Martin's patch and
re-sending his work for that one.

review_comments.author: Martin Raiber
review_comments.summary: reviewer questioned the suitability of replacing the current locking mechanism with a percpu semaphore, suggesting potential performance issues and proposing alternative solutions such as RCU lists or arenas like memory allocators
review_comments.raw_body:
Np, I was just solving for the specific problems I saw with minimum effort.

I would imagine there might be performance problems with just replacing with a percpu semaphore (e.g. with zoned).
Maybe it needs to be a RCU list? Or different arenas like memory allocators (since you are already using size classes...)?

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 2/2] btrfs: commit after deleting an unused block group if system space is low

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 2/2] btrfs: commit after deleting an unused block group if system space is low

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where deleting multiple unused block groups in one transaction fails due to lack of system space, resulting in an -ENOSPC error. To mitigate this issue, the patch introduces a mechanism that commits a single transaction after deleting a single unused block group when system space is low. This approach ensures that freed space is available for subsequent allocations, making it more likely to succeed even with limited system space.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 1/2] btrfs: allocate additional SYSTEM space earlier

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 1/2] btrfs: allocate additional SYSTEM space earlier

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch allocates additional system space earlier to prevent a large number of block groups from being deleted simultaneously, which can lead to ENOSPC errors. The current behavior reserves system chunks only when the space left is smaller than the reservation for a single chunk tree update, leading to tens of thousands of chunks being accumulated on very large file systems. To fix this, the patch introduces a new function `system_space_target` that computes a rough bound on the bytes needed to modify every leaf in the chunk tree and allocates system space when it is half full. This change should only affect very large file systems.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 0/2] btrfs: ENOSPC fixes for unused block groups

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 0/2] btrfs: ENOSPC fixes for unused block groups

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses ENOSPC issues in Btrfs by allocating system space earlier and eagerly committing deletions when the system chunk is at risk, thereby preventing allocation failures caused by unused block groups.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, mirroring the existing implementation in memcg. The new struct page_counter_stock_pcp preserves the functionality of its memcg counterpart and adds a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended, but rather a copy of existing code from memcg.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be stock-aware, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving the same semantics as try_charge_memcg's greedy charge attempt and refill behavior. The function now takes two new parameters: may_batch, which preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios, and nr_charged, which reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge. This change is intended to improve memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high without affecting existing functionality.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more flexibility in managing memory usage. The transition is done while preserving the legacy user-visible memory <= memory+swap invariant. The patch also removes unused memcg code and prepares for future work on introducing additional page counters without affecting cgroup v2 users.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock (bank) to the memsw page counter in Linux's memory control system, allowing it to operate independently of the main memory bank. The patch introduces new functions for scheduling and draining the stock, ensuring that failed allocations do not replenish the newly attached memsw stock. It also preserves user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant by reporting memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes as the larger raw value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock abstraction from mem_cgroup to page_counter, improving scalability and performance for future page_counters. The change simplifies try_charge_memcg code and allows each page_counter to opt into its own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages.
